summary: Defines how to put characters outside ISO-8859-1, and language information, into parameters of HTTP header fields, which otherwise cannot carry them. It reuses an encoding profile from the MIME mechanism in RFC 2231. This RFC is now historic and was replaced by RFC 8187.

plainLanguage.summary: HTTP headers are like labels that only allow a small set of letters. This gives a way to write other letters and languages on them. It is old now and has a newer replacement.

questions: how to encode non-ascii characters in http header parameters
how to encode non-ascii in http headers
subtitle: Encoding non-ASCII characters and language info in HTTP headers

tldr.problem: HTTP header field parameters use a limited character set and cannot carry non-ASCII characters or language information needed for internationalization.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5987 defines a way to encode character set and language information into header parameters using an extended syntax with percent-encoding, following a profile of RFC 2231 designed for MIME but adapted for HTTP.
tldr.outcome: Web servers and clients can now transmit filenames, descriptions, and other parameters with international characters in HTTP headers, with UTF-8 or ISO-8859-1 as mandatory character sets.

today: RFC 5987 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 8187.

sections.title: The Character Set Problem
sections.content: By default, message header field parameters in HTTP messages can only contain characters from the ISO-8859-1 character set. This limitation means header parameters cannot carry characters from other alphabets or Unicode characters needed for international use. For example, a filename with Chinese characters or a description in Russian cannot be transmitted directly in an HTTP header parameter. RFC 2231 solved this problem for MIME headers, but MIME and HTTP have different constraints. RFC 5987 specifies an encoding suitable for HTTP that reuses key concepts from RFC 2231 but adapts them to HTTP's rules.
sections.plainLanguage: HTTP headers are like address labels on an envelope. They only allow certain letters. This RFC explains a special code to write other languages on the label.

sections.title: The Encoding Syntax
sections.content: The extended parameter syntax uses an asterisk at the end of the parameter name to indicate it contains encoding information. The parameter value has three parts separated by single quotes: the character set name, optional language information, and the encoded value. For example: title*=UTF-8'en'%e2%82%ac%20rates specifies UTF-8 encoding, English language, and the percent-encoded value (where %e2%82%ac is the euro sign in UTF-8). Producers must use either UTF-8 or ISO-8859-1 character sets; these are the only mandatory-to-implement options. Characters not in the allowed token set are encoded as bytes using the specified character set, then percent-encoded as in RFC 3986.
sections.plainLanguage: The code works like this: first you say what language the letters are in (UTF-8 or another), then you say what human language it is (like English), then you write the special code for each letter using percent signs.

sections.title: How It Works in Practice
sections.content: A simple header parameter without special characters looks normal: foo: bar; title=Economy. If the title contains the pound sign (£, Unicode U+00A3), it can be encoded as: foo: bar; title*=iso-8859-1'en'%A3%20rates, where the pound sign becomes the single byte A3 in ISO-8859-1, then percent-encoded as %A3. For the euro sign (€, Unicode U+20AC) which needs multiple bytes in UTF-8, the encoding would be title*=UTF-8''%e2%82%ac%20rates. When multiple instances of a parameter exist (one in plain text, one extended), the extended syntax takes precedence. This allows senders to provide a fallback for legacy recipients that do not understand the extended syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to write a pound sign in ISO-8859-1, you write %A3. If you want the euro sign in UTF-8, you write %e2%82%ac. Old readers might ignore the fancy version and use the plain one instead.

sections.title: Security and Implementation
sections.content: The ability to transport non-ASCII characters creates character spoofing scenarios where a displayed value may appear to be something other than it actually is (for example, lookalike characters from different languages). Additionally, UTF-8 decoding has known attack vectors. Recipients should handle encoding errors robustly, whether by ignoring the parameter, stripping non-decodable sequences, or substituting a replacement character. When multiple language variants of the same parameter are provided, they must be equivalent, otherwise different language versions could enable spoofing attacks. Header field specifications using this extension should define how to handle precedence and error cases.
sections.plainLanguage: When you read special letters, you need to be careful. Some letters from different alphabets look the same but are not. Also, broken codes need to be handled carefully without crashing.
